articles.title: Marc Gual enciende la Champions: "Está difícil, pero lo vamos a intentar"
articles.standfirst: El '9' español suma cuatro goles y dos asistencias en seis partidos con el Kairat
articles.summary: El '9' español suma cuatro goles y dos asistencias en seis partidos con el Kairat
articles.body: El Kairat dio la sorpresa la temporada pasada clasificándose para la Champions League por primera vez en su historia. Una misión (casi) imposible que aspira a reeditar gracias a los goles de Marc Gual (Badalona, 1996). "Venía de no jugar demasiado en el Río Ave, recibí varias ofertas y, tras hablar con varios compañeros que ya conocía, me decanté por la del Kairat. Es un club que lucha por títulos y por competir en Europa, que cuenta con muy buenas instalaciones y la propuesta económica también era buena. Todo era positivo, así que decidí probar y, por ahora, la verdad es que todo va muy bien", asegura a MARCA. Los 8.000 kilómetros que separan Almaty de España parecían la principal barrera: "El tema de la distancia era lo que más me tiraba para atrás. El viaje, con los dos perros, se nos hizo un poco largo a mí y a mi mujer, pero es lo único malo. Almaty es una ciudad muy 'top': moderna, bien comunicada... Tiene de todo y se vive muy bien. Hemos acertado".  Sin embargo, el exatacante de Espanyol 'B', Sevilla Atlético, Zaragoza, Girona, Real Madrid Castilla, Alcorcón, Dnipro-1, Jagiellonia Bialystok, Legia y Río Ave ha caído de pie en el Kairat: acumula cuatro goles y dos asistencias en seis partidos.  "Hasta el momento está yendo todo muy bien. He marcado goles, he repartido asistencias y, desde que llegué, no hemos perdido. El estilo de juego me viene bien: queremos tener el balón, atacar mucho, crear ocasiones...", subraya Marc Gual antes de ahondar en las exigencias tácticas de Rafael Urazbakhtin: "El míster me pide es que aparezca entre líneas para crear ocasiones y en zonas de finalización para rematarlas. Ése es mi fuerte y para lo que estoy aquí".  Marcó, también, en la victoria por 2-1 sobre el Sutjeska Niksic montenegrino en la primera ronda previa de la 'vieja' Copa de Europa. "Entrar en Champions está difícil. La temporada pasada lo consiguieron por primera vez en su historia, pero lo normal es no conseguirlo porque el nivel es muy alto y tenemos que pasar cuatro rondas previas".  La posibilidad de perpetrar un nuevo milagro, sin embargo, está ahí: "Lo vamos a intentar. Ojalá pasemos esta primera ronda para asegurarnos entrar en Europa, aunque no sea Champions, pero jugar, al menos, la Europa Legue o la Conference. Vamos paso a paso y ya llegará lo que tenga que llegar", confiesa Marc Gual, que ya compitió en el Viejo Continente con el Legia. Con el Legia, precisamente, batió su récord anotador: marcó 19 goles en la 2024-25. No va por mal camino... pero no quiere desviar el tiro. "Siempre uno quiere marcar goles, pero lo principal es ayudar al equipo, jugar, tener minutos... El resto, si el equipo va bien, irá viniendo. Ojalá pueda superar los 19 goles que marque con el Legia, pero prefiero ganar la Liga y jugar en Europa que superar mi propio récord".  Hoy, nuevamente, les espera el Sutjeska Niksic. "Los partidos de Europa y de la Liga son diferentes. En la Liga somos el equipo grande, dominamos el juego y creamos ocasiones. En Europa los partidos son más igualados y los rivales más fuertes. Hay equipos que te dominan, algo que en la Liga no pasa tan a menudo. Tenemos que adaptarnos. Eso es lo que hará que podamos entrar en Europa", reconoce el '9' español del Kairat. Con Marc 'Goal' será más fácil.

articles.title: Marc Gual y el Kairat quieren volver a estar en Champions
articles.standfirst: El conjunto kazajo selló el pase a la segunda ronda de clasificación contra el Sutjeska
articles.summary: El conjunto kazajo selló el pase a la segunda ronda de clasificación contra el Sutjeska
articles.body: El Kairat ya hizo historia la temporada pasada al convertirse en el segundo equipo kazajo en disputar la Champions tras el Astana en 2015. Sin embargo, no se conforman con ello y están dispuestos a pasearse de nuevo por los mejores campos del Viejo Continente. Un gol del ariete español Marc Gual en el tiempo de descuento amarró el triunfo contra Sutjeska en el partido de ida. "Entrar en Champions está difícil. La temporada pasada lo consiguieron por primera vez en su historia, pero lo normal es no conseguirlo porque el nivel es muy alto y tenemos que pasar cuatro rondas previas", repasaba en MARCA el ex de Río Ave en la previa del choque de vuelta. De nuevo, Rafael Urazbakhtin lo ubicó como principal referencia en el Kairat. Sin embargo, fue el jovencísimo Ismail Bakbolat (2008) quien anotó el 0-1 justo antes de abandonar el campo. El Sutjeska estaba contra las cuerdas... y firmó su sentencia con la expulsión de Raznatovic y posterior tanto de penalti de Jorginho terminaron de amarrar el pase. En la siguiente ronda ya espera el Omonisa Nicosia en el tortuoso camino que le restan a Marc Gual y el Kairat hasta poder plantarse en la fase liga definitiva de la Champions 26-27. También sellaron la clasificación el Universitatea Craiova Rumanía), el Klakvik (Islas Feroe) y el Egnatia (Albania).

articles.title: Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK?
articles.summary: Economics editor Faisal Islam examines whether the north-west city can be a template for the entire country.
articles.body:
It was just five months ago when Andy Burnham retreated to his mayor's office in Manchester, having been blocked by Labour's ruling executive from standing for parliament.

When I met him there a few weeks later, he told me he planned to deal with his disappointment with some ambitious plans for his city region.

Burnham told me he wanted to appeal directly to Fifa to host the final of the women's football World Cup in 2035 Manchester instead of Wembley. "Imagine how electrifying that is for any girl growing up in the north of England," he said.

He said he was also joining forces with other mayors for a "Great Northern" Olympic bid across the north of England, and a plan was also afoot to host the Ryder Cup in Bolton. Sports bodies needed "re-educating" about the rest of the country, he said.

Manchester has already poached the Brit Awards from London after half a century in the capital.

Big, bold gestures like these tell part of the story of what has happened in the city. Burnham's civic ambition is a byproduct of Manchester's status as the fastest-growing city economy in the country. As Burnham prepares to become prime minister, will he be able to apply the same model to the whole of the nation?

Even before Burnham returned to parliament in June, there has been talk of Manchesterism as a political-economic philosophy that offers a programme for national transformation, rooted in a critique of a currently unresponsive, over-centralised British state.

The city has a long history of blending the freest of free markets with a strong social spirit. Manchester's cotton traders championed free trade and liberal economics, at the same time as the emergence of the co-operative movement, the trade unions and the Suffragettes. Even the Manchester Ship Canal, the emblem of monopoly-breaking free trade, required local government intervention backed by the workers.

But for an understanding of contemporary Manchester, you need to go back to the summer of 1996.

Andy Burnham had left the north-west of England by then. He told me how when he first looked for a local media job after graduating in the early 1990s, all he could get was a role as an unpaid reporter on the Middleton Guardian.

"I had to do what so many people of my generation, born in the 60s or 70s in the north-west of England had to do to get on in life," he said. "We had to go south."

By 1996, Burnham was an MP's researcher. That year, back in Manchester, the IRA detonated the largest bomb in the UK since World War Two, devastating the city centre,

The reconstruction in the aftermath of the attack marked the start of Manchester's ascent from the doldrums of de-industrialisation. The essential idea provided by a group of local political, cultural and business leaders, and an architect called Ian Simpson, was that the city centre should be reshaped by demolishing, not repairing, many of the damaged buildings.

From disaster could then arise a great opportunity to reshape the city's geography and economy. Council leader Sir Richard Leese and his top civil servant, the late Sir Howard Bernstein set the tone for a variety of bold centrally driven strategic plans that were actually largely delivered by private capital and then significant international investment.

The council leadership was ruthlessly focused on transforming brownfield industrial sites. The private sector would go nowhere near them, but the council de-risked those investments with public money. It also sometimes stepped in to tide projects over during financial crises.

At the end of this process, private capital poured in, lining up the cranes and the hard hats. The council offered a flexible interpretation of requirements to build a proportion of "affordable housing", sometimes effectively waived, sometimes met by funding building in cheaper areas of the city.

Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, which has funded some of these projects, and who is on the board of the University of Manchester, says Manchester's success story over the past 20 years was "built on there being a clear plan the private sector can get behind".

Such a shift would have been unthinkable a generation ago. The model of Manchester's city centre development has succeeded in creating a critical mass of population, housing, jobs and service sector activity that has allowed it to turn its significant undergraduate population into a goldmine.

According to the mayor, more people from London had moved to Manchester (13,000) than the other way round (11,800) in the latest set of internal migration figures.

He put this down to a flow of young workers into the Manchester city centre service economy.

In a reverse from the 1990s, "no-one here has to leave to get on in life", Burnham told me. "And in fact, there's a net inflow of young people from London."

Manchester now retains over half its graduates, more than any other city apart from London, according to the Centre for Cities, and Manchester also attracts almost as many young graduates as it produces.

Tom Beahon, the CEO of Manchester-based sports brand Castore, who has not been shy about criticising some of the government's business policies, told our Big Boss podcast earlier this year that the mayor had helped "attract inbound investment, making it a place that students want to stay after they graduate from the fantastic universities". That in turn means more businesses want to launch in the city, he added.

It is a case study in agglomeration effects - the economic power of locating similar types of jobs close together. And if its infrastructure can keep up, Manchester's economy will continue to fly.

Andy Burnham is a product of this Greater Manchester and spent his decade as its first mayor trying to shape it. As Andy Spinoza, the foremost chronicler of Manchester's turnaround, puts it: "Burnham jumped into a moving car, and by the end he was driving it."

But what else is there to Burnham beyond driving that moving car?

While he has managed to ascend to the Labour leadership and the cusp of No 10 without revealing his wider policy plans, there is a fairly recent text already out there. In 2024 with his fellow north-west regional mayor, Merseyside's Steve Rotherham, he published a book called Head North: A Rallying Cry for a More Equal Britain.

It was the basis for Burnham's speech earlier this month on Manchesterism and remains his national political-economic-constitutional prospectus. The 10-point plan to "rewire" the country argues that better "homes, transport and jobs" across the country can only come from "a new set of principles and rules for the running of the British state".

What underpins this is a determination to tear up two formulas that have long formed the backbone of how UK governments allocate money. The first is the Treasury's Green Book, which decides infrastructure spending and which has traditionally valued existing areas of high growth and land value the most. In Burnham's view, this drags investment in transport to the south of England.

The tangible example of all of this can be found on Platforms 13 and 14 of Piccadilly station in central Manchester. The only east-west train link for both the city centre and the North's main international airport is here, and it is often jam-packed with trains and 40,000 daily passengers attempting to cross the Pennines, or get to the airport, or to Merseyside. Burnham has long advocated for an underground four-platform "Kings Cross of the North" with a northern version of London's Elizabeth Line.

He relays a story about his time as chief secretary to the Treasury in 2007 when he was told: "No project in the north passed the Green Book, Minister." He told me the same in 2020 when there were murmurings of reform to the formula. Chancellor Rachel Reeves pursued pilot projects to change the approach that could favour local investment.

In the book, Burnham also advocates tearing up the Barnett formula, which allocates public spending, topping up spend for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland so they do not lose out to England as a whole. The effect, Burnham argues, is that the north of England is left squeezed in a "pincer".

In Head North and his recent speech, Burnham points to Germany's "Basic Law", with its duty of "equivalent living standards" across the regions. Such a law, he argued, would protect local government and give regions a right to be consulted on long-term decisions.

Burnham also advocates significant constitutional change, including a form of proportional representation and the replacement of the House of Lords with a "Senate of the Nations and the Regions", alongside devolution of powers over large swathes of public services to regional level.

On Net Zero he proposes a "Northern Way", which subsidises the transition, retrofits, cutting bills, and building exportable locally owned industry. He contrasts this with a "Whitehall way", which he characterises as bans, charges and taxes that hit the poorest.

The actual policy consequence of this will have to reckon with rising global energy prices, pressure on household budgets, and some impatience from North Sea energy interests to pump more oil and gas. There are some contradictions in for example, full tax and spend devolution for every region. Would the south-east get to keep the taxes it raises? Some aides recently played down any changes to the Barnett formula amid concerns from Scottish politicians.

The fundamental difference between running a city region and a country is the need to raise the entire spectrum of tax revenues to fund spending. Or to borrow more money. The picture is rather constrained on both right now. Manchester has been agile in attracting private capital to build infrastructure, especially housing, partly because it had to. Can that stretch across the whole country?

With Manchester's cotton traders in mind, I asked Burnham back in February if he considered the Manchester model to be politically left or right - an example of statism, perhaps?

"When it comes to right versus left, well, we've always been very pro-business, pro-enterprise here. We want people to succeed individually and businesses to succeed, but give back at the same time," he said.

Some campaigners say that the dash for the gleaming towers and spires in the centre has left behind much of the rest of the region, and that the centre of Manchester is becoming a mini-London. While Burnham has criticised decades of "neoliberalism" and the "trickle-down effect", the reality is it has been core to the Manchester model.

At the same time, Margaret Thatcher's 1985 bus deregulation has been reversed and over the years public money from central and local government, from the EU, as well as from the partly council-owned airport, has been spent on trams - a nod to the importance of spreading the proceeds of growth in the centre around the region.

To greater or lesser degrees Burnham has floated more "public control", cost of living support, small business rates relief, and higher infrastructure investment and higher defence spending. They sound difficult to reconcile with sticking to promises to limit borrowing and not raise major taxes.

For example, the Defence Investment Plan is "funded" by cuts to capital investment in transport, energy and elsewhere. These are precisely the areas that Manchesterism would suggest might get more central capital investment.

Burnham the mayor has beaten the drum for the new Liverpool-Manchester Northern Powerhouse Rail and the high speed Manchester-Birmingham line he worked up with former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street. But what will Prime Minister Burnham do?

And what about the paused Brexit reset? There was a deal ready to go for closer relations at a UK-EU summit originally planned for next week. The government had started to explore different red lines for the next Labour manifesto and a turn back towards Europe's single market. Does he go with Remainy Manchester? Or do the feelings of his Leave constituency, Makerfield, trump all?

NatWest's Paul Thwaite says there could be a "powerful recipe for sustained growth" from the private capital that flows from "long-term certainty and genuine collaboration". There isn't, however, a "single blueprint" from Manchester or anywhere, he says. For devolution to work "the institutions, the leadership and the commercial capability matter as much as the powers themselves".

Burnham in his speech quoted the famous line attributed to Tony Wilson in the film 24 Hour Party People: "It's Manchester, we do things differently here." Now it's time to reveal what exactly it means for the nation.

Clarification 31 July: We have amended a passage in this article to make clear that Manchester Piccadilly station is Greater Manchester's only link for trains going from east to west across the Pennines, and that Platforms 13 and 14 are for services to the east coast, to Merseyside and the city's airport.

articles.title: El delantero español que quiere volver a hacer historia en la Champions: "Aquí solo vale ganar"
articles.standfirst: Marc Gual, reciente fichaje del Kairat Almaty kazajo, habla de su nueva vida en Marcador Internacional de Radio MARCA
articles.summary: Marc Gual, reciente fichaje del Kairat Almaty kazajo, habla de su nueva vida en Marcador Internacional de Radio MARCA
articles.body: Marc Gual ha iniciado una nueva etapa lejos del fútbol español. El delantero catalán, de 30 años, ha fichado este verano por el Kairat Almaty, vigente campeón de Kazajistán y uno de los clubes habituales en las rondas previas de la Liga de Campeones. En una entrevista concedida a Radio MARCA en el programa Marcador Internacional, el atacante explicó los motivos que le llevaron a aceptar una aventura "desconocida", aunque reconoce que el crecimiento del club en Europa terminó de convencerle. "El año pasado no fue el mejor que he tenido, jugué menos de lo que deseaba y había que cambiar de aires. Salió esta oportunidad y nos cuadró todo. Es un equipo que pelea por títulos y que puede jugar competiciones europeas", explicó Gual, que la pasada temporada militó en el Rio Ave portugués. Su estreno no ha podido ser mejor. El Kairat ya ha superado la primera eliminatoria previa de la Champions tras eliminar al Sutjeska, con un gol decisivo del propio delantero español en el encuentro de ida. Ahora espera el Omonia de Nicosia, un rival de mayor entidad en el camino hacia la fase de liga. "Sabemos que repetir lo del año pasado es muy complicado, pero si vamos partido a partido siempre es posible. El Omonia será un rival difícil, aunque creo que tenemos equipo para competir e intentar volver a entrar en la Champions", señaló. El Kairat adquirió notoriedad internacional la pasada temporada al convertirse en el primer club kazajo en disputar la fase de liga de la Champions, donde incluso recibió la visita del Real Madrid. Aquella histórica participación ha cambiado la dimensión del club. "Los compañeros que estuvieron el año pasado dicen que todo ha cambiado. La gente te reconoce por la calle porque juegas en el Kairat y el club ha crecido muchísimo gracias a esa participación europea. Eso sí, la presión aquí no es como en otros países", reconoció. Porque, según explica Gual, la verdadera exigencia está en el campeonato doméstico. "El objetivo principal es ganar la Liga. El Kairat ha conquistado las dos últimas y es el club grande del país. Eso es lo que te permite volver a jugar las previas de la Champions". Más allá del fútbol, el delantero también habló de su adaptación a Kazajistán, un cambio radical tanto por la distancia como por la cultura. Se ha trasladado a Almaty junto a su mujer y sus dos perros, una decisión que no fue sencilla. "Era la principal duda que teníamos. Son ocho horas de vuelo y otro continente completamente diferente. Pero la ciudad nos ha sorprendido mucho, vivimos muy tranquilos y el club nos ayuda en todo con un traductor para los jugadores extranjeros", explicó. Eso sí, el mayor desafío llega con los desplazamientos europeos. "Para jugar fuera tenemos que viajar dos días antes. Entre las seis o siete horas de vuelo y el cambio horario necesitas tiempo para adaptarte", concluyó un Marc Gual que ya suma un gol en Champions y tres tantos en la liga kazaja en sus primeras semanas con el Kairat.

articles.title: Cesc, el trampolín del Como: "Cuando llegué nos cambiábamos en un bar y ahora jugamos la Champions"
articles.standfirst: El entrenador español prepara una revolución para competir en Europa
articles.summary: El entrenador español prepara una revolución para competir en Europa
articles.body: El Como prepara el más difícil todavía. La victoria sobre la Cremonese (1-4) certificó la clasificación de los 'lariani' para la Champions por primera vez en su historia.  "Es un logro enorme, conseguido con jugadores jóvenes. El presidente me dio las riendas y tomé muchas decisiones. Cuando llegué hace cuatro años, como jugador, no teníamos centro de entrenamiento y nos cambiábamos en un bar. Ahora, en cambio, estamos en Champions", recordaba Cesc Fábregas. Un hito para el que ya han puesto las bases. “No se podía dar por sentado que uno de los mejores entrenadores de Europa, como Cesc, decidiera quedarse con nosotros en el Como, al igual que Nico Paz, uno de los mejores talentos del contiente”, reconoce el director deportivo, Carlalberto Ludi. Jugar en Europa implica una importante reforma a todos los niveles, empezando por el estadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia. No sólo se aumentará el aforo, también se ampliará el terreno de juego dos metros de ancho. La plantilla sufrirá un importante cambio. La Champions únicamente te permite disponer de 17 fichas libres —sin importar nacionalidad— en la lista A. El resto, hasta 25, sólo se puede completar con futbolistas formados en la Federación a la que perteneces. Esto supone un problema. El Como, la temporada pasada, sólo contaba con dos italianos en nómina: Vigorito y Goldaniga. Entre los dos jugaron 14 minutos en Serie A. “Fichar jugadores en Italia es un problema debido a la rigidez de los métodos de pago”, asegura el presidente Mirwan Suwarso, que ha pagado seis kilos al Cantanzaro por Liberali. “El sector juvenil es crucial. Debemos permitir que el talento crezca con paciencia”, subraya Cesc. Se han ido 'pesos pesados' (Diego Carlos, Sergi Roberto, Alberto Moreno...) y han seguido pescando en LaLiga: Luis Milla y Andrés Cuenca. Vendrán más. “Si no estás preparado para jugar en el Bernabéu o el Allianz, te arriesgas a encajar seis goles. Me gusta entrenar a jóvenes, pero debemos traer gente con experiencia”, insiste Cesc. La Champions le espera.

articles.title: The World Cup is over, long live the World Cup: A look back at one of the best tournaments ever
articles.summary: And just like that, the 2026 World Cup is over. After 308 goals were scored during 104 matches in 16 host cities across three continents, it was Spain that lifted the trophy.
articles.body: Note: This story first appeared in The Beautiful Game by CNN Sports, our daily newsletter on all things World Cup. While we’re saying goodbye for now, we will be back for the European domestic club season. See you then! And just like that, the 2026 World Cup is over. After 308 goals were scored during 104 matches in 16 host cities across three countries, it was Spain that lifted the trophy. And while the final wasn’t exactly one for the neutral, it was fitting that the best team in the tournament won in the end. But while La Roja supporters around the world celebrated the country’s second title (Spanish editor’s note: my headache and I can confirm this occurred in North London), everyone else was left reflecting on an emotional, record-breaking, superstar-studded edition of the tournament. For years, there were so many concerns around this World Cup. Would it be safe? Would the locals care? Would it be a waste of money? And while those critics were proved right at times, the 2026 edition can still be considered a resounding success. And that’s not down to the politicians or governing bodies; it’s down to the millions of fans who flocked to North America to party with one another. It’s down to the superstars who turned up and performed at the highest level and to the tournament minnows who punched well above their weight. So, in our last World Cup edition of this newsletter, it only feels right to remember some of the most magical moments. The Main Thing: And the award goes to… Before Spain got its hands on the main trophy, there were also several individual awards handed out at the end of yesterday’s final. France’s Kylian Mbappé was named the winner of the Golden Boot after scoring 10 goals – becoming the World Cup’s all-time top scorer in the process. Spanish defender Pau Cubarsí was named the best young player, Unai Simón was awarded the Golden Glove for best goalkeeper and midfielder Rodri won the Golden Ball for player of the tournament. But while those official awards have already been decided, we at The Beautiful Game wanted to recognize some of our own winners. Treat this as CNN’s World Cup Oscars. You may disagree with some decisions, but that’s OK because I’m quite tired. Best Game Sorry, Spain fans, but it certainly wasn’t the final. Fortunately, though, we were treated to some incredible soccer matches over the past month and change. The first game that springs to my mind is England’s heroic effort against Mexico in the Estadio Azteca. Down to 10 men, fighting altitude and fervent home support, the Three Lions somehow clung on against the co-host to reach the quarterfinals. We then had the likes of Cape Verde drawing against Uruguay, 2-2, and then the Blue Sharks again pushing defending champion Argentina to extra-time in the Round of 32. But, on balance, I think we’re given this to the Albiceleste’s 3-2 comeback against Egypt in the Round of 16. It had everything. Controversy galore, brilliant goals and a Lionel Messi-shaped miracle comeback. At least you won something, Argentina fans… Best Goal This is usually a hard category to decide, but I actually think it’s quite simple this year. The award goes to Cape Verde’s Sidny Lopes Cabral for his wondergoal against the Albiceleste in the knockout stages. There are a few reasons why this was so special. First, the strike itself was superb. He first beat his marker out wide before cutting in and bending his effort into the top corner of the net. Then consider the context. The goal was in extra-time against Messi’s Argentina. All of a sudden, Cape Verde fans started to believe in miracles. And then there was his celebration. Cabral was so excited that he ran into the crowd looking for someone he knew to celebrate with. It was an iconic moment that will be remembered for quite some time. Biggest Upset This one has caused some debate within the team. Not to keep banging on about Cape Verde, but not many expected the tiny island nation to play so well, so most of its results look like upsets on paper. Then you have Curaçao, the smallest nation to ever play in the competition, who managed to hold onto a draw against Ecuador in the group stages. But after much deliberation, I’m giving this to Paraguay for beating Germany in the Round of 32. Now I know the Germans are struggling a bit with their current crop of players, but they definitely should have beaten Paraguay on paper alone. The South Americans, though, somehow went ahead in the match and relied on a fighting spirit to restrict Germany to only one goal in reply. After defending that draw with their life, the Albirroja then beat the European powerhouse on penalties (something that very few have done before). Quote of the Day A quick break from the awards show to give you a sense of what the World Cup win meant to Spain. These are the words from goalscorer Ferrán Torres, who won the final for his country after scoring the only goal of the game. Torres, 26, said he felt the entire population of Spain behind him as he lashed his extra-time effort into the back of the net and it couldn’t have happened to a more deserving person. Torres – one of Barcelona’s key men up front – had been having an awful tournament, missing a plethora of chances throughout the campaign and being benched after starting against Cape Verde. The Barça attacker came through in the clutch, bringing joy to an entire nation that had almost abandoned him. WATCH: Fans react to Spain winning the World Cup If you still don’t understand how much soccer means to fans around the world, then just watch this. Spanish supporters filled the streets of Madrid to celebrate the country’s second World Cup title after the team beat Argentina. CNN en Español’s Pau Mosquera was in and amongst the bedlam in the capital. Awards continued Biggest Controversy Right, back to the awards and, sadly, a few contenders for this category. Even before a ball was kicked, there were plenty of headlines. First, Somali referee Omar Abdulkadir Artan was denied entry into the United States, meaning his dream tournament came to an end before it even began. Then we had the appalling treatment of the Iranian national team, which had to change training bases at the last minute and then fly between its base in Mexico and the US in order to play its games. But the moment that caused the biggest uproar was the red card decision around USA star Folarin Balogun. More notably, the fact that Donald Trump took it upon himself to try to overturn the decision. It was a stark insight into how those with power see the world. In no way should Trump be getting involved in such a thing, and there is even less reason FIFA should have listened. It contributed to a sad ending for the US team, which played so well at times and inspired a new generation to get into the sport of soccer. No real winners for this category, then. Biggest Star And finally, which of the players stood out the most. We have a few contenders for this one. Messi, of course, was superb and rolled back the years to produce some mesmerizing performances. We then have Mbappé who showed once again why he’s probably the most effective player at international tournaments – there is just something special about his game at World Cups and European Championships. Then we have to consider the likes of England’s Jude Bellingham who was just immense for the Three Lions and Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha who became an overnight star. But, after plenty of discussion, I’m going to surrender to the internet memes and give this award to Erling Haaland. The Norwegian striker did the business on the pitch, let’s get that straight first. He took his team to the quarterfinals, beating five-time champion Brazil on the way and scoring some big goals. But his larger-than-life personality also endeared him to people across the world, many of whom didn’t even watch the games. The Haaland memes and video clips were everywhere. Lookalike events popped up all around the world and people fell in love with the 25-year-old’s approach to, well, everything. “I’m quite happy with my life,” he said after bowing out of the competition. Lifetime Achievement Well, one last category – because that’s what these sorts of award shows do, right? It’s basically just an excuse to recognize Lionel Messi for everything he has done for soccer and answer the question that many people have: Is he now retiring from the international game? In truth, we don’t know yet. At 39, he’s clearly not able to compete physically against the best in the world during an entire match. But he does still show flashes of brilliance that make you think he can keep playing. The tears at the end of the final, though, suggest where his mind might be at. He has nothing left to prove and has won everything he possibly can. He’ll probably take some time to reflect but, yes, there is a chance that’s the last time we see Messi in an Argentina jersey. But we have said that before. Don’t fear, though. The Argentine is still contracted to play for Inter Miami until 2028, so he’ll surely honor that and be back on a soccer pitch again soon. The Final Whistle: The Beautiful Game bids farewell… for now And just a final note from me as we wrap this newsletter up for the World Cup. There has been so much to talk about, break down and reflect on during this tournament and I hope you got something out of this daily drop. We hope to be back in the not-so-distant future once the world’s biggest domestic leagues get back up and running, but more on that soon. For the time being, we’re off to sit on a beach for a couple weeks and reflect on what has been one of the best summers of sport. ¡Adios! The Trophy Lift: CNNers show their love for the World Cup And the last word goes to CNNers from all around the world who tuned in to watch all the action unfold. We hope you enjoyed the tournament as much as we did.

articles.title: La 'obra maestra' de Julio Velázquez: "Llegar a fase de grupos, aunque sea en Conference, sería un exitazo"
articles.standfirst: El estratega español aspira a seguir avanzando en Champions con 'su' Levski
articles.summary: El estratega español aspira a seguir avanzando en Champions con 'su' Levski
articles.body: Julio Velázquez (Salamanca, 1981) puso fin la temporada pasada a la mayor dinastía en activo del planeta fútbol, las 14 Ligas consecutivas que acumulaba el Ludogorets. “No siento que sea mi mayor obra. En los 29 años que llevo entrenando he vivido grandes momentos”, reconocía a MARCA. El exentrenador de Poli Ejido, Villarreal, Murcia, Betis, Alcorcón, Alavés y Zaragoza, entre otros, condujo al Levski a poner fin a ¡17 años! de sequía en Bulgaria. 'Novias' no le han faltado, pero se ha mantenido fiel al banquillo del Georgi Asparuhov. “Recibí diferentes opciones en distintos contextos que podían resultar atractivas tanto a nivel deportivo como económico, pero tengo contrato y me siento querido y valorado. Soy feliz y, aunque ya se ha conseguido hacer historia, pienso que todavía se puede serguir construyendo. Eso es algo bonito y atractivo”, afirma el técnico español. Consiguió superar al Ludogorets a pesar de tener un presupuesto cinco veces inferior y confía en repetir con un español en sus filas: Álex Centelles ha llegado libre del Almería. “El mercado es muy dinámico y dura muchísimo. Al empezar a competir en Europa tan pronto tenemos que estar atentos a posibles entradas y salidas. Las diferencias a nivel presupuestario siguen existiendo, pero mi responsabilidad es sacar el máximo rendimiento en base a las herramientas que tenemos a nuestra disposición”, subraya. Su Levski superó ampliamente al Borac Banja Luka (1-5) en su estreno en Champions. Ahora le espera el Universitatea Craiova... pero la posibilidad de jugar la Fase de Grupos de la Liga de Campeones por primera vez desde la 2006-07 sigue pareciendo lejana. “El equipo compitió muy bien en la 1ª ronda previa. Ahora tenemos un rival muy duro y debemosofrecer nuestra mejor versión. El Levski lleva casi 20 años sin jugar una fase de grupos de una competición europea. El año pasado estuvimos cerquita de lograrlo. Si esta temporada lo logramos, en cualquiera de las tres competiciones, sería un exitazo”, reivindica Julio Velázquez. El triunfo ante el Universitatea Craiova tendría un valor añadido: “Si pasamos una ronda más, sí que nos garantizaríamos jugar, como mínimo, la Fase de Grupos de la Conference, lo que ya sería algo absolutamente extraordinario. Vamos día a día con el objetivo de seguir compitiendo en Champions: los chicos se lo han merecido”. Una cosa tiene clara: lo que funciona no se toca. “La temporada pasada conseguimos romper la hegemonía del Ludogorets gracias al gran trabajo de los jugadores e intentamos, en cualquier competición, mantenernos fieles a nuestra identidad. Es decir, ser un equipo muy proactivo con y sin balón. En Europa debemos ajustar detalles para sentirnos cómodos y competir de una manera fiable, pero intentamos llevarlo a cabo”, insiste Julio Velázquez, que podría rubricar un 'cuadro' de Champions.

articles.title: Kvaratskhelia se aferra a la 'vía Kevin Keegan' para soñar con el Balón de Oro
articles.standfirst: El inglés fue el último futbolista que ganó el galardón en año de Mundial sin participar en el torneo
articles.summary: El inglés fue el último futbolista que ganó el galardón en año de Mundial sin participar en el torneo
articles.body: ¿hasta qué punto debe influir el torneo más importante del fútbol en la elección del Balón de Oro? Históricamente, la Copa del Mundo ha servido para impulsar candidaturas, pero no ha sido una garantía de éxito. De hecho, la propia organización del premio ha querido recordarlo una vez concluido el Mundial de 2026. En un artículo publicado tras la final, el Balón de Oro recuerda que, aunque conquistar la Copa del Mundo ayuda, no garantiza el premio. De hecho, desde que el galardón se abrió a futbolistas de todo el mundo en 1995, sólo cuatro de los siete ganadores en años de Mundial fueron también campeones del mundo. La conclusión del propio artículo es todavía más reveladora: “Para ganar el Balón de Oro hay que haber sido el mejor jugador de la temporada, no solo del Mundial”. Ese criterio vuelve a situar en la conversación a futbolistas como Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, ausente del Mundial pero autor de una de las temporadas más completas del fútbol europeo. El georgiano firmó una campaña sobresaliente con el Paris Saint-Germain, registrando 19 goles y 10 asistencias en 48 partidos, consolidándose como uno de los grandes líderes del campeón de Europa. Su candidatura al Balón de Oro se construyó, sobre todo, en la Champions League, competición en la que terminó con 10 goles y seis asistencias en 16 encuentros y fue elegido 'Mejor Jugador de la Temporada' de la UEFA Champions League. Desde el 'playoff' de acceso a los octavos de final frente al Mónaco hasta la final participó directamente en 10 goles (seis tantos y cuatro asistencias). Además, en la final provocó el penalti que permitió al PSG igualar el encuentro antes de conquistar la primera Champions League de su historia. Y existe un precedente histórico que refuerza esa misma idea. En 1978, en pleno año de Mundial, Kevin Keegan conquistó el Balón de Oro después de una extraordinaria temporada con el Hamburgo, a pesar de que Inglaterra ni siquiera se había clasificado para la Copa del Mundo. Casi medio siglo después, la reflexión vuelve a ser la misma: si el Balón de Oro debe reconocer al mejor futbolista de toda la temporada, y no únicamente al más brillante del Mundial, la candidatura de Khvicha Kvaratskhelia mantiene argumentos más que suficientes para seguir entre las grandes favoritas al galardón.

articles.title: Yaya Touré, un estreno de Champions: "Los jugadores son las estrellas"
articles.standfirst: El exjugador del Barcelona debutó como entrenador del Slovan Bratislava en la previa
articles.summary: El exjugador del Barcelona debutó como entrenador del Slovan Bratislava en la previa
articles.body: Yaya Touré (Bouaké, 1983) llevaba tiempo preparándose para dar el salto a los banquillos. Ejerció de asistente en Olimpik Donetsk, Akhmat Grozny y Standard antes de convertirse en la 'mano derecha' de Roberto Mancini en Arabia Saudí.   Ahora, tras hacer sus 'pinitos' en la Academia del Tottenham, afronta su primera aventura en solitario como entrenador del Slovan Bratislava. "Mi objetivo era traer a una persona y una personalidad que haya vivido el mejor fútbol del mundo. Me causó una impresión maravillosa: tiene un gran deseo y motivación para triunfar como entrenador", reconocía Ivan Kmotrík Jr., director general del club.  "He tenido la oportunidad de trabajar con entrenadores excelentes en el pasado, pero anhelaba crear mi propio proyecto. Tengo mucho que aprender. Soy consciente de mis limitaciones", apunta el marfileño, que ha 'pasó por las manos' de Guardiola, Pellegrini, Mancini, Rijkaard... El ex de Barcelona, Manchester City, Mónaco y Olympiacos, entre otros, 'aparca' los más de 700 partidos, 127 goles, 73 asistencias y 18 títulos que coleccionó a lo largo de su carrera como jugador: "Lo tengo claro. Los jugadores son las estrellas. Están en el campo y han ganado las últimas ocho Ligas de forma consecutiva; es a los que todos miran".  La propuesta, eso sí, es innegociable. "Quiero que dominemos el juego y seamos agresivos cuando no tengamos la posesión. Nuestro principal objetivo debe ser marcar goles. No soy el tipo de entrenador que se toma los partidos con cautela: soy un ganador y me encanta ganar", confesaba a 'Dennik Sport'. Su estreno oficial llegó a lo grande, en Champions. El Slovan Bratislava de Yaya Touré -su hermano Kolo fue ayudante de Guardiola en el Manchester City- debutó con victoria sobre el Iberia 1999 (0-2) en la ida de la segunda ronda previa. "La actitud de los jugadores fue excelente. Estoy satisfecho, trabajamos bien, pero todavía tenemos margen de mejora. Hay que entender que este es un proceso que llevará tiempo. Estamos cambiando gradualmente la forma y la filosofía de juego, pero ya estamos viendo cosas buenas", afirma. Aún queda la vuelta y otras dos previas por delante, pero la Champions -ya la ganó con el Barcelona en 2009- le espera.

articles.title: Luke Littler dazzles in Blackpool as frightening World Matchplay Darts form continues: 'Good luck to Dirk...'
articles.summary: Is Luke Littler in the best form of his life? His run at the World Matchplay is proving that may be the case as he progressed to the semi-finals with dominant a win over Josh Rock; you can watch the World Matchplay live on Sky Sports in Blackpool until July 26
articles.body:
Littler came into Blackpool as the reigning and defending champion with the expectations on his shoulders to deliver.

He has and then some. The numbers are jaw-dropping:

113 average in first round (second-highest at Matchplay behind Phil Taylor's 114.99 in 2010)

109 average in second round and quarter-finals

If his heights were not already incomprehensible, they have gone up a notch.

Not only that, Littler knows he can dominate.

"I feel really good up on the stage. Preparations beforehand have gone really well, just relaxing, playing and relaxing again. I am just glad I can perform on the biggest stages," Littler said.

"I feel like I can. Obviously a 109 average, a 113 and back down to a 109 average comes with the big finishes. The scoring power is there as well.

"As long as I can keep it up, I'm sure I will dominate. Next game, let's get it back up to the 113s."

That next game will see Dirk van Duijvenbode become the next player charged with attempting to stop Littler in his tracks.

Up to this point, Littler's win over Rock marked the 27th time in a row he won a match that went over 20 legs.

Not only that, Littler continues his quest to become the first player since Michael van Gerwen in 2016 to go back-to-back in Blackpool, and the world No 1 currently holds the World Darts Championship, UK Open, Premier League and Masters. He is also defending the Matchplay, Grand Slam, Grand Prix and the Players Championship Finals.

With all the in mind, Sky Sports Darts' Mark Webster has a simple message for the Dutchman when he takes on the best player in the world on Saturday, live on Sky Sports : "Good luck."

"He can play in spells. I say spells because he's been doing it all tournament. I was delighted for Josh because it was an improved performance and a 101 average but he lost by nine legs so it just shows how good Littler is," Webster said.

"He looks comfortable in every scenario. Good luck to Dirk on Saturday.

"It's 111 tournament average. He's played almost 60 legs. He's just too good! He's focused and relaxed.

"He's by far the best player in the world. It's frightening form."

What is happening on Friday at the World Matchplay Darts?

The quarter-finals continue, live from 7.30pm on Sky Sports Main Event and Action.

Gian van Veen and James Wade will do battle in the quarter-finals for a second year in a row, with the world No 3 looking to avenge his loss to 'The Machine' in 2025.

Then, Gerwyn Price faces Ross Smith. Smith went through to the quarter-finals after Cameron Menzies withdrew from their second-round match in the fourth leg due to illness.

Who will win this year's World Matchplay Darts? Luke Littler is be defending his title and you can watch all the action on Sky Sports. Stream darts and more top sport with NOW .

articles.title: Jurgen Klopp: Germany appoint former Liverpool boss as new head coach to replace Julian Nagelsmann
articles.summary: Jurgen Klopp returns to management as the new Germany head coach; Klopp left Liverpool in 2024 because he was "running out of energy", having won six trophies at the club in nine years; the 59-year-old had been working as Red Bull's global head of football; Klopp succeeds Julian Nagelsmann
articles.body:
Klopp has returned to management on a contract that runs until the end of the 2030 World Cup after leaving Liverpool in 2024 because he was "running out of energy" , having won six trophies in nine years at the club.

The 59-year-old was unveiled on Friday and issued a stark warning to journalists after his predecessor Julian Nagelsmann faced intense scrutiny and criticism from the media.

"It is my mission to make the national team squad a better team and hope the pool for me to choose from will be bigger, but it is not something I am doing against you, I am doing it for you. It is an honour," he said.

"I will be remunerated very graciously and if tomorrow Jurgen Klopp is s***, I will be gone. But if the DFB says let us discontinue the job, then that's it. And if you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace, I'll be gone. I'll just turn away. I know there are other countries where national team head coaches are treated even worse. I love this job but I am also ready to call it quits if needs be.

"Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any 'career' after the national team. This is the pinnacle, the high point of my footballing career as a coach. I will give everything I've got, and I have the best possible assistant coaching team."

Klopp was the first person the DFB turned to when Nagelsmann resigned after a disappointing World Cup ended with a penalty shoot-out exit to Paraguay in the last 32.

But Klopp has also warned his appointment won't guarantee success and that expectations need to be adjusted.

"Jurgen Klopp being in the job doesn't automatically mean we're going to be world champions," he said.

"Success is performance vs expectations. We need a new set of expectations. Many people have asked themselves, are we as good as France? If the answer is no, then that is not necessarily true. If the question is, do we have players like Dembele, Barcola, Mbappe? Then the answer is no, we don't, but we can still beat them.

"We don't want to play like Argentina, Spain, England or France. We want to play like Germany, do it the German way but very intense. Are we the number one team at the moment? No, we aren't; I accept that. Would we be happy to be the number two team? Then people would say we aren't number one.

"At the moment, we have 11 teams ahead of us. Yes, we can beat them, but for this to happen, you need to play very good, intense football."

His first game in charge is against the Netherlands in the Nations League on September 24.

Klopp won the Champions League, Premier League, Club World Cup, FA Cup and League Cup twice at Liverpool.

After a six-month break, Klopp was appointed head of global soccer at Red Bull and later stated that he had no desire to return to club management.

Klopp's former Liverpool assistants Pep Lijnders, who recently left Manchester City after Pep Guardiola's departure, and Peter Krawietz are part of the coaching staff, along with Sven Bender, who played under the German at Borussia Dortmund.

Per Mertesacker, who stepped down as Arsenal's academy manager after eight years at the end of last season, will become Germany's sporting director in January, replacing Andreas Rettig.

'Klopp is the perfect manager at the right time - and he wants to make changes'

Sky Germany's Patrick Berger speaking on Sky Sports News:

"For Klopp, it's very important to make some things different to the former coach of the German national team, Julian Nagelsmann. He wants to have a direct relationship to the players, he wants to see them directly in the stadiums.

"This was something Nagelsmann was criticised for in the past because he didn't see or visit Kevin Schade at Brentford, he didn't visit Yann Aurel Bisseck at Inter, he didn't visit Niclas Fullkrug at West Ham. This is a point Klopp wants to change. He wants to bring all the people in Germany behind him.

"He has a list of around 57 to 60 players, he said, that he finds very attractive. The kind of players who have the chance in future to play for Germany. He said every player who is able to wear the Germany shirt should be aware that he may be calling.

"The German public have reacted very well because he's the perfect manager, he's here at the right time and is someone who has the credibility, the energy after two years out of being in this daily job as a head coach. We are a proud football nation and this makes the people in Germany believe we can be successful again in the future."

articles.title: Luke Littler: World Matchplay defending champion believes he can dominate like Phil Taylor ahead of semi-final
articles.summary: Luke Littler stormed into the semi-finals of the World Matchplay with a thumping win over Josh Rock and has set his sights on dominating the sport in the same fashion as Phil Taylor; you can watch the World Matchplay live on Sky Sports in Blackpool until July 26
articles.body:
A scintillating Littler progressed to the semi-finals of the World Matchplay on Thursday with a dominant 16-7 win over Josh Rock , averaging 109.57 with a 53 per cent success rate on the doubles.

On Saturday 'The Nuke', who scored 17 180s against Rock in Blackpool, will face Dirk van Duijvenbode in the semi-final - live on Sky Sports .

The world No 1 is aiming to become the first player since Michael van Gerwen in 2016 to go back-to-back in Blackpool, with few betting against him.

Following his win, Littler was asked by Sky Sports if he is confident he can dominate the sport in the same fashion as all-time great Phil Taylor did.

Littler said: "Yeah, I feel like I can. My averages of 113 and 109 come with the big finishes and the scoring power is there as well with the 180s. As long as I can keep it up, I'm sure I will dominate."

He was then asked about the prospect of being the first player in history to approach £3m on order of merit.

Littler replied: "I checked the rankings the other day. I think if I beat Dirk [van Duijvenbode], then I will go into that £3m mark.

"As long as I'm playing like this and producing numbers, it's going to take something special from another player to beat me. I've just got to keep going."

Littler currently holds the World Darts Championship, UK Open, Premier League and Masters titles.

He is also defending the Matchplay, Grand Slam, Grand Prix and the Players Championship Finals.

Such is his form there are suggestions he could be set for the greatest ever Matchplay.

On talk of the prospect, he said: "I wouldn't say I'm aware of it. I saw something yesterday that Gezzy [Gerwyn Price] is up in the ranks for most legs played.

"In this competition you don't want to be at the top, you want to be down at the bottom. You don't want to win by two clear legs, you just want to get the job done. As long as I perform like that, I'll be happy."

Immediately after Thursday's win, he said: " I feel really good up on the stage, preparations beforehand are going really well, just relaxing, playing, relaxing again. I'm just glad I can perform on the biggest stages."

articles.title: World Matchplay darts: Gerwyn Price issues title warning to 'ruthless' Luke Littler after reaching Blackpool semi-finals
articles.summary: Luke Littler remains pre-tournament favourite to defend his title at the World Matchplay; Gerwyn Price faces Gian van Veen in Saturday's semi-finals as he looks to reach his first Blackpool final since 2022; watch throughout the weekend live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Price booked his first World Matchplay semi-final since 2022 with a 16-12 win over Ross Smith at the Winter Gardens, where the 'Ice Man' fired a 102.78 average and closed out victory with a four-leg burst.

The Welshman faces world No 3 Gian van Veen in the last four, with the winner of that semi-final progressing to face either Littler or Dutchman Dirk van Duijvenbode in Sunday's best-of-35 leg final.

Littler defeated Price in every Premier League fixture between them this season and a final-set decider in the World Masters semi-finals, while 'The Nuke' remains unbeaten in PDC major matches over 20 legs since his 2024 World Championship final loss.

The world No 1 remains overwhelming favourite to become the first player since Michael van Gerwen to defend his World Matchplay crown, having posted a 109.57 average in his win over Josh Rock, although Price insists he can be stopped.

"I think there's a lot of players that can get to that [Littler's] level," Price told reporters after his quarter-final win.

"Is there anyone who can do it as long as him? I think I can and I think there's a couple of players, but he's ruthless at the minute - these 109, 110 averages just look so easy for him.

"I think some players play into his hand and just let him play with his rhythm. It's horses for courses, and sometimes you have to play your game, you have to play the game and you have to play the moments.

"Sometimes, people make it a little bit too easy for him."

Price built a commanding 12-8 lead over Smith in a quarter-final where he threatened to pull further ahead, then found himself level at 12-12 until finishing strongly to reach the last four.

"I was delighted with the way I played the majority of the game, but there's a couple of legs that I let slip and could have come back to haunt me in the end," Price added.

"I'm thinking I should be 13-7 or 14-6 or whatever it is, because I did waste opportunities and probably shouldn't think like that. I'm just happy to get a win, but frustrated a little bit."

Van Veen admitted he needs to improve after his quarter-final victory over 16-13 James Wade, where he posted a 93 average and also blew a four-leg advantage before closing out victory.

"It felt very poor!" Van Veen admitted to Sky Sports. "My scoring was so terrible. I was so lucky James wasn't scoring as well and my finishing got me through. A win is a win.

"The 118 finish - I really needed it. It was a tight battle but I'm glad I got the job done. Hopefully tomorrow I will be a lot better."

The 2026 Betfred World Matchplay continues at the iconic Winter Gardens on Saturday, with the two semi-finals being played over the best-of-33 to decide who progresses through to Sunday's best-of-35 final.

Defending champion Littler continues his bid for back-to-back titles when he faces Van Duijvenbode, through to the last four at this event for the first time, with Price playing Van Veen in the opening semi-final.

articles.title: Luke Littler reaches new heights with World Matchplay run to remember: 'What can other players cling onto now?'
articles.summary: Sky Sports Darts' Mark Webster believes Luke Littler produced the greatest World Matchplay campaign ever seen and has backed him to complete a clean sweep of the remaining majors in 2026
articles.body:
Littler capped off a record-breaking week with a dominant 18-9 win over Gerwyn Price in the final, setting a new record average in a final of 111.53.

He also broke his own record for the number of 180s hit across the tournament, improving his 64 in 2025 to 66 in 2026.

The victory in Blackpool saw Littler become only the fourth player in tournament history to win back-to-back titles, and the first in a decade to achieve the feat. It also keeps alive his bid to complete a clean sweep of the major titles across the year.

He already has the World Darts Championship, UK Open, Premier League, Masters, and now the Matchplay. He is also defending the Grand Slam, Grand Prix and the Players Championship Finals later this year and hunting a European Championship win to hold every single premier title.

For Webster, Littler's run at the Matchplay marks the greatest major display in the history of the sport and is another sign that the world No 1 is increasingly likely to eventually hold every major trophy the sport has to offer simultaneously.

"This is what I keep saying - what do the other players cling on to now? Where is the weakness? What do you do," Webster said.

"He is playing fantastic at the minute and he is making his opponents miss. It is a recipe for dominance.

"The tournament average has been in the back of his mind. He is setting himself a challenge inside a challenge.

"Winning a major is a huge thing to do but he is setting little challenges within that.

"It is going to get to the point where he is going to be leaving 170s and things like that because he is dominating contests.

"He is just in a completely dominant mood. He trusts everything he does. You just have to admire it. We probably think he can't get better but he is going to try.

"He is going to keep craving tournament averages - he just has that will to win.

"This has to be the greatest campaign at a major, doesn't it? This has to be it. If you look at the stats alone, he has a tournament average of 111.

"It is an incredible achievement and it is one that in 12 months time he will try to eclipse.

"I half expect it [for him to win every major in 2026].

"I don't see where you are going to get him. European champs maybe? Players championship? I am just throwing things out there.

"It is going to be tough for the rest of them."

Time to 'take stock' as Littler sends a message to the pack

For those chasing Littler down, the question is what do you do next?

Records have fallen, he has dominated in Blackpool, and has already set his sights on what he needs to do next in order to continue this remarkable run.

And it truly is remarkable - his last defeat in a major tournament that went beyond 20 legs came against Luke Humphries in the World Darts championship back in 2024.

Can they stop what seems inevitable? Webster thinks it will take "new standards" to even get close to him.

"It just sends out a message now to the rest of the pack of the standard you have to reach to get anywhere near him.

"Every player from this event will take stock of what happened.

"Someone like Luke Humphries, it won't wash for him being knocked out in the first round so he will need to refocus.

"Michael van Gerwen has got a huge end to the year. I think he is down at world No 7 now which feels strange to say.

"There is some work for him to do there now - he was a finalist at the World Darts Championship two years ago so there is some more money coming off.

"After every tournament you have to take stock, look at what you need to improve on, and get ready for what is the business end of the year now."

The next PDC ranked TV major is the BoyleSports World Grand Prix from September 28-October 4 at the Mattioli Arena, Leicester, live on Sky Sports . Littler returns as defending champion after last year's victory over Luke Humphries in the double in, double out event.

The Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton (November 14-22) and the World Darts Championship (December 10-January 3) are also both live on Sky Sports, with Littler looking to retain his titles in both events. Stream darts and more top sport with no contract.

articles.title: World Matchplay Darts: Luke Littler draws fresh Phil Taylor comparisons after historic record-breaking Blackpool victory
articles.summary: Luke Littler posted the highest tournament average in World Matchplay Darts history to successfully defend his title in Blackpool; Littler thrashed Gerwyn Price to continue his run of winning every PDC major title in 2026 and receive fresh praise
articles.body:
Littler capped off a historic week at Blackpool's Winter Gardens becoming the first player since Michael van Gerwen to successfully defend his title, continuing his record of winning every PDC major title in 2026 so far.

The book of darting superlatives is rapidly running out of pages to describe Littler's brilliance, with the teenager continuing to climb to generational heights in the sport and overtake many records held by childhood idol Taylor.

Littler had already defended titles at the World Championship and the UK Open, plus won the Winmau World Masters, Premier League and the World Cup of Darts, with the 19-year-old now chasing more success in the months and years ahead.

"I don't think anyone has ever won every major in the calendar year and that is what we are pushing for," Littler told Sky Sports . "The family, they are always backing me a million per cent and that is what drives me on.

"I would absolutely love to be the greatest dart player there ever has been. As I have always said, I have got to win 16 of these, 16 worlds, and then have a look at whatever else Phil Taylor did win.

"I have got plenty more years. When am I going to retire? Who knows. I have still got plenty more years left in the tank."

Littler smashed the highest tournament average, posting 111.04 across his five matches to beat Taylor's 2010 previous best of 106.31, plus broke his own record of most 180s at a World Matchplay.

"I am very happy with myself and the performances, not only in the final but the past eight days, every round," Littler added. "It is crazy to say that the 109 average was my worst average throughout the tournament!"

Why time is required in Taylor comparisons

Littler may have his hands back on the trophy named after Taylor, but he would need to win every World Matchplay until 2040 just to equal the all-time title tally of 'The Power'.

In 2007, six months after Luke Littler was born, Phil Taylor made a quarter-final exit at the World Matchplay - just the second time this century that 'The Power' had been beaten on the Winter Gardens stage.

Seven years later, the week after Littler left year two of primary school, Taylor had still not lost another match at the event and was closing out a seventh consecutive World Matchplay title.

Taylor won a record 38 consecutive matches during that title streak and lost just eight times in his 24-year career at the World Matchplay, with no player since coming remotely close to beating those extraordinary achievements.

The trophy comparisons may be a mismatch but the scoring differences between the two are certainly not, with Littler posting the second-highest tournament winning average in the sport's history and just 0.5 points behind Taylor's 2009 European Championship win - despite playing over double the legs Taylor did that week

"I can still get better," Littler insisted in his press conference. "I can obviously get a lot better. Through the matches I was up to a 120 average at one point. I didn't stick at it, but maybe in a few years' time I will stick at it and go up to that when the match is finished.

"At the minute, I'm playing some of the best stuff and I've just got to keep it there."

Littler was described by Price as "one in a million" and has taken plenty of plaudits from his peers for his run to another TV title, with his success more impressive given the growing depth at the top of sport.

"Luke's dominance over the last 12 months has been very Taylor-esque and that's why he's reached that figure (£3m in prize money), which is a huge figure and one that we've never had before," PDC chief executive Matt Porter told Sky Sports .

"I don't think the mentality of the opponents is the same (as Taylor's era). 20-odd years ago, players would see getting to the final as their championship.

"You wouldn't get that answer off Gerwyn Price, you wouldn't get it off Luke Humphries, Michael Van Gerwen, Steven Bunting, Nathan Aspinall, Jonny Clayton - those guys are not here to make up the numbers.

"Luke at the moment is almost unstoppable. Nobody's ever unstoppable, but with the way he's playing, someone's really going to have to up their game if they're going to beat him."

Further title defences at the Boyle Sports World Grand Prix (September 28-October 4) and Mr Vegas Grand Slam of Darts (November 14-22) are to come for Littler, who already holds a record-breaking advantage at the top of PDC rankings.

Littler will look to claim his elusive TV ranked title at the European Championship (October 22-25), while winning all three would leave him just requiring the Players Championship Finals (November 27-29) to complete a sweep of every major and big TV event in a calendar year.

Phil Taylor's impressive 2009 season didn't contain the Premier League title or the World Cup of Darts, which didn't launch until the following year, while Van Gerwen's 2016 dominance was also missing World Cup glory. Littler has the chance to surpass both with his campaign.

Littler has been skipping ProTour events during the season to leave qualification for the Players Championship Finals in doubt, although his latest win - and thoughts of claiming all the majors in the same - has changed his schedule plans over the coming months.

"Coming into the tournament I'd won every major so far so this is what I wanted to do," Littler explained. "I have been checking the Pro Tour rankings - whoever is in 64th (final qualification spot) just keeps going up and up!

"I know there is four (Players Championship events) in Leicester I have got to go to now. If I don't qualify I will get grilled and if I qualify I will get grilled anyway, so who knows what is going to happen."

Littler has already cemented himself as one of the darting greats in just over two and a half years as a professional. The thought of him getting even better in pursuit of more records is a terrifying - but exciting - prospect.

articles.title: Luke Littler: Target Darts explain the science behind World No 1's phenomenal success
articles.summary: "He's back-to-back world champion, what he could do in the sport is entirely up to him" - James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says the world is Luke Littler's oyster; you can watch the BoyleSports World Grand Prix live on Sky Sports from Sept 28 to Oct 4 in Leicester
articles.body:
Littler has spearheaded darts' surge towards the mainstream since he broke on the scene with his debut run to the 2024 World Championship final as a 16-year-old.

Darts manufacturer Target Darts has supported the global superstar since the age of 12. In February 2024, the teenager signed a multi-year mega-deal reported to be worth up to £20 million - the most lucrative the sport has ever seen.

Littler possesses a generational talent when it comes to playing darts and Sky Sports pundit Wayne Mardle has said "he's probably the most natural naturally gifted player I've ever seen in my life".

Since the moment the Warrington-born star first held a dart, he's become a record-breaker and history-maker.

James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says both the company and Littler are "aligned" in where they want to see the future of darts go.

Speaking at an event in which Target have set out a vision to inspire 100 million people to play darts by the end of the decade, he explained the process of how Littler sat down with chairman Garry Plummer, the design team, and engineers to build darts to perfect his game.

"I think some of the inspiration was drawn from Adrian Lewis' darts and the pixel grip, which is a unique grip that Target has and that worked its way into building up Luke's original G1," said Tattersall. "That was the barrel, but over the years Luke's tweaked it and challenged us to improve it. The point length has changed, the shaft and flight have changed to a K-Flex system before his first World Championships."

F-Flex is a one-piece flight and shaft innovation that screws into the back of the barrel.

Tattersall explained: "What it helps you do is when you're throwing darts together in such tight groupings like Luke does, the thing you want to avoid is that dart coming in and deflecting off the dart that's already in the board and the K-Flex helps reduce those deflections substantially.

"And longer points - it's like the balance of the dart and how it flies and how it lands through the air. I think another part of it is it keeps the barrel section of the dart further away from the treble and that creates more space in the board."

"His talent is all down to him," says Tattersall. "I think when you're talking about the equipment, we're talking about making Luke comfortable with all of that talent and giving him the right equipment that he's confident with to use and just to get those last few percentages, but Luke's an extraordinary player regardless."

With two world titles in three visits to Alexandra Palace, and 14 major titles to his name, Littler is well on his way to joining Phil Taylor as a legend of the sport.

The problem for his rivals is that he is still getting better after the Warrington star crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 to retain his Betfred World Matchplay title in Blackpool on Sunday.

Littler was in imperious form as he set a new record for the final with an average of 111.53, lifting his average for the tournament as a whole to 111.04 to break Phil Taylor's previous high mark of 106.31.

The win keeps Littler on course for a clean sweep of trophies in 2026 having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters.

Littler's management have invested in sports psychologists, nutritionists, performance coaches, and biomechanics in order to get the most out of their talent, and the teenager has benefitted in every area to help support his game.

"Mentality is absolutely key. We want to protect the players. The stage is lonely up there, and darts is a gruelling sport," Tattersall said.

"It's a bit like a penalty shootout, but every single time you're throwing a dart. It's such a closed skill, and it's so repetitive. Your mindset's got to be really, really clear, and you get those big momentum swings, you think you're about to checkout the double, you miss by a millimetre, your opponent throws in a big 170 checkout, and that's a punch in the stomach. It's how do you recover from that for the next leg? That's sports psychology, and it's crucial in all sports. I don't know why it's a surprise that it should not be in darts."

'We want to learn about action - not create robots'

With biomechanics, the cameras observe how a player throws darts, with sports science data helping ways of working on the technique in order to improve.

Target have ideas but Tattersall insists implementing them will not turn the Luke Littlers of this world into robots.

"That's the last thing we want to do," he said. "What we want to do is discover and learn about the sport, and learn about that action, because why is it that there are different throwing techniques?

"If you look at something like golf, where you know suddenly you come along with the Vardon grip [or overlapping grip], and that becomes almost the only way to hold a golf club.

"I think the high jump has got that really famous example of how the sport, science, innovated, [Fosbury flop], you ended up with that kind of one technique point.

"I think there will always be different ways of throwing a dart, and there will be different ways of improving those different styles, and maybe that particular style is because you're tall, and maybe that particular style is because you've got longer arms, we don't know yet, but that's what we're going to find out, and then use that data accordingly."

Zoe Burton, Chief Transformation Officer at Target Darts, says Littler is already inspiring the next generation with his natural talent, although the company are slowly moving towards a performance technology system, which is currently being tested on a number of players.

"If you look at a young person and you think of their journey as they get into a sport, you need an inspiring player - that person who they look up to - and can almost aspire to be. Luke Littler provides that," said Buton.

"You need a natural talent, but that gets you so far. Then it's determination and I think psychology as well.

"What makes a star player become a great and world-class player is actually their ability to focus under pressure and make those doubles It's never going to be robotic."

articles.standfirst: El atacante del Barça reconoce que ha necesitado ayuda y que su coach personal ha tenido trabajo extra para ayudarle a salir adelante
articles.summary: El atacante del Barça reconoce que ha necesitado ayuda y que su coach personal ha tenido trabajo extra para ayudarle a salir adelante
articles.body: "Ha sido el peor verano de mi vida. Estaba en el mejor momento, todo salía bien y llegó la lesión. También se aprende de estas situaciones, pero es cierto que este verano lo he pasado muy mal.   He salido adelante gracias a mi familia, mi compañera y mis amigos. He necesitado ayuda. Ya tenía antes, pero mi coach me ha ayudado mucho a salir adelante", las palabras de Fermín en el programa a Tot Costa de Catalunya Ràdio desde el stage de pretemporada del Barça en Inglaterra son definitorias.  Fermín reconoce en la entrevista que los primeros partidos de España se los tuvo que ahorrar. "Los primeros partidos de la selección española en el Mundial no los vi. No podía. Quería estar allí en el Mundial. Que quede claro que me ha hecho muy feliz ver a mis compañeros ganar el Mundial. En el tramo final del Mundial ya lo pasé algo mejor y decidí ir a ver la final en directo a Nueva York". "Me encuentro cada día mejor. No tengo molestias, que es importante. Si todo va bien, en el Gámper podría jugar ya unos minutos. La intención es volver de esa lesión con más motivación. Creo que estoy muy preparado. Ya he demostrado cómo puedo ayudar al Barça y esta próxima temporada tengo que seguir igual". "El sueño de la Champions es compartido con todo el equipo. Los dos últimos años hemos estado cerca. Esta temporada puede ser buena. Llevamos tres años jugando juntos y hemos vivido muchas cosas. Siento que estamos preparados para ganar la Champions. Ganar la tercera liga consecutiva es difícil. articles.title: Luke Littler insists 'clean sweep very much on' as he attends Warrington mural unveiling days after World Matchplay win
articles.summary: Luke Littler attends unveiling of mural he "didn't want to see" in Warrington just four days on from storming to World Matchplay victory; 'The Nuke' has his sights set on unprecedented clean sweep amid stunning form
articles.body:
The 2026 PDC World Championship winner was frightenedly good in Blackpool, beating darts legend Phil Taylor's Matchplay record average of 106.31 with 111.04.

"I'm feeling very good," Littler told Sky Sports at the unveiling of his mural in Warrington on Thursday. "With performances like that, not many can stop me. Obviously, a tournament average of 111 was really, really good."

The 19-year-old has won every PDC title in 2026 so far - the World Championship, World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup and now the World Matchplay.

As it stands, he could still achieve an unprecedented clean sweep of eight ranking titles in the calendar - and Littler admitted that record is on his mind going forward, starting with working on qualifying to defend his Players Championship Finals title.

"The clean sweep is very much on," he said. "I think you can only look at what's coming up. For myself now, I can't go and say 'I'm going to win the World Championships'. That's in another five or six months.

"You've just got to look at what's in front of you. I've got a nice two-week holiday to Orlando tomorrow as well to look forward to. I think the clean sweep, it's very much on.

"As long as I qualify for Minehead, whether I win the World Series, the European, it's all coming up. It's a busy end of the year, but we'll see."

If a clean sweep was achieved, where does Littler think it would rank in terms of sporting achievement?

"For darts, I think it would be up there with probably one of the best," he said. "No one's ever done it. That's what I'm going for. I like to break all these records."

Littler's mural was unveiled in his hometown Warrington just four days on from breezing past Gerwyn Price to win yet another title in Blackpool.

The teen darts sensation signed his name on the artwork, took time to pose with fans for photos and played darts in front of the crowd present.

However he is still keeping himself grounded, both mentally and physically.

"[The mural is] very good," Littler said. "I actually saw it yesterday or the day before. I didn't want to see it, but they've done a really good job.

"I'm really happy. Someone said you can see it from miles away. It's that big, it's that tall.

"At first, they wanted me to sit on the roof. I said no chance! I'll just stand on the pavement."

Littler's next match will come in Leicester on the Pro Tour on August 25 and 26 at Players Championship 27 and 28 as he looks to secure his place at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead.
